content: Recent evidence suggests that dual therapy is recommended for the treatment of gonorrhea. For infections caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the following regimens are advised: 1. A single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone (250 mg) combined with a single oral dose of azithromycin (1 gram). 2. Alternatively, a single oral dose of cefixime (400 mg) combined with a single oral dose of azithromycin (1 gram). For Chlamydia trachomatis infections, the treatment options include: 1. Doxycycline (100 mg) taken orally twice daily for 7 days, but only if azithromycin was not included in the gonorrhea treatment. 2. A single oral dose of azithromycin (1 gram). 3. Erythromycin (500 mg) taken orally four times daily for 7 days. 4. Ofloxacin (200–400 mg) taken orally twice daily for 7 days, but only if azithromycin was not included in the gonorrhea treatment. For Mycoplasma genitalium infections, the recommended treatment is azithromycin, starting with a 500 mg oral dose on the first day, followed by 250 mg daily for the next 4 days, provided there is no macrolide resistance. Due to increasing antimicrobial resistance to azithromycin in N. gonorrhoeae and M. genitalium, as well as reduced susceptibility of N. gonorrhoeae to cephalosporins, the World Health Organization (WHO) is revising its treatment recommendations and dosages. Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is caused by pathogens such as N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, and bacteria associated with bacterial vaginosis. Facultative gram-negative rods and mycoplasmas have also been implicated. Since differentiating between these pathogens clinically is challenging and precise microbiological diagnosis is difficult, treatment regimens must cover a broad range of pathogens. WHO recommends treating sexually active women presenting with lower abdominal pain and clinical signs such as cervical motion tenderness or lower abdominal tenderness for PID during the same visit. Testing for N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, and, if available, M. genitalium is advised to support partner management. For genital ulcer disease, the most common causative agents globally are herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 (HSV-1 and HSV-2). Other frequent causes include Treponema pallidum (syphilis), C. trachomatis serovars L1–L3 (lymphogranuloma venereum), and, less commonly, Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid). Clinical differentiation of genital ulcers is often inaccurate, even by experienced clinicians, and laboratory-based etiological studies or syndromic management guided by local epidemiological data are recommended. Primary syphilis typically presents as a painless ulcer (chancre) at the site of infection, which may go unnoticed if located in concealed areas. If untreated, the ulcer heals spontaneously within 2–10 weeks, but the infection progresses to secondary syphilis. Secondary syphilis manifests with systemic symptoms such as fever, malaise, and a generalized maculopapular rash, often involving the palms and soles. Condylomata lata (highly contagious wart-like lesions) and mucous patches may also occur. If untreated, syphilis enters a latent phase, which can progress to tertiary syphilis, characterized by severe complications such as cardiovascular and neurological involvement. For genital herpes, the first episode often presents with systemic symptoms (fever, headache, malaise) and localized symptoms (pain, itching, dysuria, and tender inguinal lymphadenopathy). Lesions typically begin as vesicles that rapidly progress to ulcers, lasting up to 15–20 days. Recurrent episodes are usually milder and shorter in duration. The WHO emphasizes the importance of syndromic management for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) in settings where laboratory diagnostics are unavailable. This approach balances the benefits of immediate treatment with the risks of overtreatment, aiming to reduce STI transmission and prevent complications such as chronic pelvic pain, infertility, and ectopic pregnancy.
